facts.claim: Nestor took part in a Stanford experiment run by Dr. Jayakar Nayak, Stanford's chief of rhinology research, with Anders Olsson, a 49-year-old breathing therapist from Stockholm. Phase one: about ten days of mouth-only breathing; phase two: about ten days of nose-only breathing. Participants returned to Stanford between phases for tests.
Nostrils were blocked with silicone plugs with surgical tape over them, so no air moved through the nose. Participants ate, exercised and slept as usual.
Baseline: Nestor's X-ray showed a severely deviated septum with severe obstruction in the left nostril; Nayak sampled about 200,000 sinus cells and did endoscopic exams.

Mouth-breathing phase: snoring up almost 5,000 percent (4,820% in one account), sleep apnea averaging 25 episodes a night, systolic blood pressure up to 142 mm Hg (stage 2 hypertension), blood oxygen dipped below 85%.
Both men had higher stress hormones, higher blood pressure and reduced heart rate variability in the mouth phase; Nestor also got a bacterial nasal infection.

Nose phase: sleep apnea disappeared, snoring fell about 85 percent and stopped after two nights for both, Nestor's blood pressure returned to a healthy range (one source: 124), the infection cleared without treatment.
Caveat: single self-experimenters, two men; no peer-reviewed publication found; figures differ between press accounts.
Slow breathing: the ideal relaxed pace in the book is 5.5 seconds in and 5.5 seconds out, about 5.5 breaths a minute.

Bernardi et al., BMJ 2001: 23 healthy adults in Florence and Pavia; reciting the Ave Maria (rosary) and yoga mantras slowed breathing to about six per minute and increased variability in cardiovascular rhythms; baroreflex sensitivity rose from 9.5 to 11.5 ms/mm Hg. The authors suggested the rosary may have partly evolved because it synchronised with cardiovascular rhythms (their interpretation).
facts.source: PubMed abstract; secondary summaries connecting to Nestor

facts.claim: Bohr effect: hemoglobin gives up oxygen more readily when blood carbon dioxide is higher; when CO2 falls, hemoglobin holds on to oxygen more tightly. Described by Danish physiologist Christian Bohr around 1904.
Nestor's chapter 'Less' argues that breathing less and more slowly leaves CO2 at a healthy level; summary: 'CO2 is crucial for respiration, not just a waste product'.
Nasal breathing: the nose is the body's gatekeeper; nasal breathing supplies nitric oxide (a summary says the nose can raise nitric oxide several-fold and allow more oxygen absorption).

In the BMJ 2001 study spontaneous respiratory rate was 14.1 (SD 4.8) per minute; talking slowed it; Ave Maria in Latin and the mantra (om-mani-padme-om in the paper) brought it to close to 6 per minute; comparison also with metronome-paced breathing.
facts.source: abstract summary via search of BMJ/PubMed

facts.claim: Christian Bohr was the father of physicist Niels Bohr; in tissues working cells make CO2 and acid so hemoglobin unloads oxygen there, and re-loads it in the lungs.
Nestor chapter list: Part Two includes chapters Nose, Exhale, Slow, Less, Chewing.
